neutral_facts.value: The prosecution alleges that the accused, who was married to the victim, subjected her to ill-treatment and torture in their matrimonial home, compelling her to take her own life. The victim had a premature delivery and later became pregnant again in 1993, during which the accused provided her with tablets that resulted in a miscarriage. The victim gave birth to a child who did not survive. On the day scheduled for mediation talks, the victim committed suicide by hanging. The accused was employed as a painter in Delhi and later secured employment in Gulf countries, visiting India only four times between 1988 and 1996. The accused took efforts to mediate the differences, but the victim committed suicide on the day of the scheduled mediation. The trial court convicted the accused under Sections 498A and 306 IPC and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for seven years and a fine of Rs.50,000/-, with the sentences ordered to run consecutively. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence.

quotes.text: This appeal arises out of the judgment dated 27.11.2013 passed in Crl. Appeal No. 910/2006 by which the High Court of Kerala confirmed the conviction of the appellant/1st accused under Sections 498A and 306 IPC and also the sentence of imprisonment imposed on him.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the appellant-husband and other accused ill-treated and tortured Lillikutty, compelling her to commit suicide. The case was based on the allegations of matrimonial harassment and the subsequent suicide of Lillikutty.

quotes.text: The prosecution is that the 1st accused married Lillikutty and their marriage was solemnized on 11.2.1988 and they continued their stay in House bearing No. MP. Vlll/84 of Karulayai Amsom along with other accused, who are the father, mother and brother of the appellant. The allegation levelled is that in the matrimonial house, the appellant/1st accused and other accused ill-treated and tortured Lillikutty, compelling her to take the extreme step of putting an end to her life by committing suicide.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the trial court and appellate court did not properly exercise their discretion under Section 31 Cr.P.C. to direct that the sentences should run concurrently, and that the sentences should be ordered to run concurrently based on the facts and circumstances of the case.

quotes.text: Learned counsel for the appellant Mr. Jayanth Muthraj contended that when a person is convicted at one trial for two or more offences, Section 31 Cr.P.C. vests a discretion in the Court to direct that the punishment shall run concurrently and in the present case the trial court and the appellate court have not properly exercised such discretionary power vested in them.

legal_principle_applied.value: Under Section 31 Cr.P.C., the Court has full discretion to order sentences to run concurrently in case of conviction for two or more offences, having regard to the nature of the offences and attendant aggravating or mitigating circumstances.

quotes.text: Under Section 31 Cr.P.C. it is left to the full discretion of the Court to order the sentences to run concurrently in case of conviction for two or more offences, having regard to the nature of offences and attendant aggravating or mitigating circumstances.
